text: This lab puts the whole chapter together. A mid-sized company has been running IT support on institutional memory and a shared drive full of Word documents — some current, some years out of date, none searchable, none reviewed by anyone but whoever wrote them. They're migrating that content into ServiceNow Knowledge Management, with three real requirements: separate audiences, a real sign-off before anything goes live, and a way to catch articles that quietly go stale after the migration too.

Step one is creating two Knowledge Bases instead of dumping every imported document into one pile. A Self-Service Knowledge Base holds the public-facing content, with Can Read open to all authenticated users and Can Contribute limited to the Knowledge management team. An IT Staff Knowledge Base holds internal runbooks and escalation details, with both Can Read and Can Contribute limited to IT roles. Every imported Word document gets triaged into one of these two before it becomes an article at all.

Step two: every migrated article starts in Draft, no matter how polished the original document looked, because a document nobody has reviewed inside ServiceNow's own workflow hasn't actually been reviewed yet. A Flow Designer flow triggers when Workflow state changes to Review, firing an Ask for Approval action to the Knowledge manager role. On approval, the flow sets Workflow state to Published and stamps the Published date. On rejection, it returns the record to Draft with the reviewer's comments attached, so the author knows exactly what to fix.

Step three: migrating years of Word documents doesn't by itself stop content from going stale again, so a scheduled job runs quarterly, checking every Published article's last updated date, and flags anything untouched for twelve months or more to the Knowledge manager. That reviewer either confirms it's still accurate, which resets the clock, or sends it back through the same approval flow for a real update. Articles that no longer apply at all move to Retired, preserving their history instead of being deleted.

The order matters. Building the approval flow before the two Knowledge Bases exist leaves no clear answer for who the approver even is, since Self-Service and IT Staff content often need different reviewers. Building the quarterly review before the approval flow exists gives it nothing to route flagged articles back through. Audience segmentation, then the approval gate, then a review cadence that reuses that same gate — each step depends on the one before it.

That closes Chapter 5. Chapter 6 opens with Service Level Management Implementation — starting with SLA Definitions and SLA Conditions, the real mechanism behind every SLA breach clock this course has mentioned so far.
